questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of processing in Chapter 6?
choices: To clarify what each collected item means
To collect more material from new places
To finish every project immediately

explanation.gentle: Processing turns captured input into clearer decisions.
explanation.direct: The chapter defines processing as clarifying each collected item rather than merely storing it.
explanation.competitive: It judges the stock instead of admiring the pile.

questions.prompt: Why is a gathered in-basket still mentally heavy sometimes?
choices: Because captured items can remain undecided and unresolved
Because baskets should always be kept completely full
Because collection makes every item more important

explanation.gentle: Gathered does not automatically mean clarified.
explanation.direct: The basket still creates drag when the inputs inside it have not yet been interpreted and routed.
explanation.competitive: Raw stock can stay heavy even when it is centralized.

questions.prompt: How does the chapter say you should process the basket?
choices: By scanning the whole pile several times first
By taking one item at a time
By waiting until all items feel familiar

explanation.gentle: One-item processing is the chapter's working rhythm.
explanation.direct: Allen's rule is to clarify the item in front of you before moving to the next one.

questions.prompt: Talia keeps glancing at a yellow note, a voicemail slip, and a printed request in the same tray. What is the best Chapter 6 response?
choices: Pick one item and decide what it is before touching the others
Keep reviewing all three until they feel more familiar
Add more labels to the tray before making any decisions

explanation.gentle: The chapter wants one-item clarification, not broad scanning.
explanation.direct: Processing begins when one input gets a clear decision instead of the whole tray being reviewed again.
explanation.competitive: Judge the note in hand, not the whole pile at once.

questions.prompt: What is the load-bearing decision split in this chapter?
choices: Urgent versus non-urgent
Actionable versus non-actionable
Big project versus small project

explanation.gentle: The chapter asks whether the item requires action.
explanation.direct: Actionable versus non-actionable is the main boundary that removes ambiguity from raw input.
explanation.competitive: Every input has to declare its side of the action line.

questions.prompt: Keira has mail, a receipt, and a reminder card on the counter. What Chapter 6 move matters most first?
choices: Deciding which items require action and which do not
Putting all three back in the basket for later familiarity
Turning every item into a calendar appointment

explanation.gentle: The chapter begins by clarifying the type of response each item needs.
explanation.direct: The actionable split is what lets mixed home inputs stop sitting there as vague possibilities.
explanation.competitive: Make each piece pick a side.

questions.prompt: A student keeps flipping through the same dorm desk stack without shrinking it. Which principle applies most directly?
choices: The stack should be scanned faster
Each handout should be processed one at a time
The stack should stay full until the semester ends

explanation.gentle: The chapter replaces broad review with item-by-item decisions.
explanation.direct: Processing the stack serially prevents recognition from masquerading as progress.
explanation.competitive: One page, one verdict, or the stack keeps hiding.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with putting a half-decided item back into the in-basket?
choices: It makes the basket too neat
It preserves raw ambiguity inside the intake point
It automatically turns the item into reference

explanation.gentle: The item stays unclear and keeps the basket mentally heavy.
explanation.direct: Chapter 6 treats undecided return trips as a sign that processing has not actually happened.
explanation.competitive: Raw stock just got sent back to the warehouse.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter treat repeated rereading as fake progress?
choices: Because repeated exposure can leave the same uncertainty unchanged
Because every item should be read only once in life
Because processing works only with digital inboxes

explanation.gentle: Recognition alone does not reduce ambiguity.
explanation.direct: Rehandling can keep an item familiar while leaving its status exactly as unresolved as before.
explanation.competitive: Warm attention is not a decision.

questions.prompt: If the in-basket is empty in the Chapter 6 sense, what question naturally comes next?
choices: How should the clarified items be placed into the right buckets?
How can more loose material be left uncaptured?
Why should decisions be delayed from now on?

explanation.gentle: Once the inputs are clarified, the next issue is where they belong.
explanation.direct: Processing prepares the items for the organizing chapter by turning them into clear decisions first.
explanation.competitive: Once the stock is judged, the bucket question takes over.
